claim: Nishi states that the paper's phonemic transcription follows Okell (1995), Three Burmese Dialects (and differs from Okell 1969), while Written Burmese forms in braces use Duroiselle's literary transliteration with modifications. The slash-delimited outputs are source-specific traditional phonemic forms, not project IPA gold. Nishi explicitly states in footnote 3 that the examples themselves are quoted from Okell (1969), Reference Grammar §§17–20; the notation convention follows Okell (1995).
scope: Nishi 1998 p.253, introductory note, PDF lines 37-46

claim: Nishi proposes a four-stage historical account involving (1) voicing of nonaspirated stops/affricates/sibilants, (2) atonicization of some non-initial syllables, (3) a second voicing rule applying to C1, and (4) later voicing of aspirated stops/affricates. This is Nishi's explanatory historical model, not a universal synchronic rule sequence.
scope: Nishi 1998 pp.254-255, PDF lines 132-157 and 218-236

claim: For Standard Old Written Burmese, Nishi distinguishes -h with sonorants as a marker of voicelessness (a unit phoneme/voiceless or aspirated sonorant in his account) from the actual consonant clusters -r, -l, -y and -w, which he calls medials. This is a historical romanized analysis, not a direct classification of modern Myanmar Unicode signs.
scope: §1.3 Initial Consonant Clusters, pp.660-661; PDF lines 84-105

claim: Nishi identifies a medial -l- in Old Written Burmese alongside -r-, -y- and -w-. He proposes that -l- was later replaced by -y- after velars and by -r- after bilabials in Middle Written Burmese, with exceptions; this is a historical correspondence, not a modern grapheme-to-phoneme rule.
scope: §2.1.1 Medials, p.663; PDF lines 152-159

claim: Nishi states that -r- and -y- represented distinct medials in Middle Burmese and merged into -y- sometime in Standard Early Modern Written Burmese; some modern dictionaries consequently retain alternative Cr~Cy spellings. This merger must be kept separate from the modern Unicode medial-letter inventory.
scope: §2.1.1 Medials, p.663; PDF lines 156-159

claim: Nishi's tentative Great Consonantal Shift account for the 18th/early 19th centuries includes Cr- > Cy- and r- > y-, with other ordered changes; he cautions that dialects may show different ordering and that the development was not as neat as the scheme. This is a historical model, not a synchronic modern Yangon rule.

Nishi's Table 3 compares Old Burmese velar and bilabial clusters with Written Burmese, Standard Burmese, Arakanese, Tavoyan, Intha and Minor Taungyo. Reflexes of clusters containing historical -r-, -l- and -y- differ across dialects; some forms alternate, and Nishi warns that standard-variety interference and hypercorrection complicate correspondences. This evidence rules out a simple universal modern medial-to-sound mapping.
scope: Table 3, p.673; PDF lines 708-823

claim: Okell explicitly distinguishes Written Burmese (WB) from Standard Burmese as spoken language (SB), and compares each regional dialect against both systems. A WB spelling must not be treated as a direct phonetic representation of SB or of a regional dialect.
scope: Foreword and abbreviations, pp.1-2; PDF lines 7-24

claim: Okell reports that Arakanese preserves the WB r/y distinction, while Standard Burmese has merged WB r with y in speech. He cautions that Arakanese is not simply a more ancient or purer version of SB; both have undergone different mergers and splits. The specific Sit-twe variety is the high-prestige reference for his Arakanese description.

Okell's Intha phoneme inventory includes medial /y/, /l/ and /w/ with distributional restrictions; the comparison with WB and SB shows Intha /l/ clusters where Standard Burmese has no equivalent medial /l/. The Intha medial /l/ is dialect-specific and must not be projected onto SB/Yangon.

Okell's Tavoyan inventory includes medial /l/ alongside /y/ and /w/; he explicitly describes /-l/ as a lateral medial consonant not present in Standard Burmese. The listed combinations are restricted by onset class and are not a universal Burmese medial inventory.

Okell describes the dialect text transcriptions as phonemic, but explicitly allows selected allophonic alternatives when closer to actual pronunciation; Intha also varies the written symbol for medial /-l-/ or /-r-/ according to realization. These are source-specific phonemic/transcription conventions, not an independently adjudicated project IPA gold set.
scope: Arakanese text note §2.4, p.37; Intha text note §3.4, p.79; Tavoyan text note §4.4, p.119; PDF lines 1523-1533, 3700-3704 and 5462-5463

claim: The Arakanese material in Okell's study is principally Sit-twe District speech; Okell says it has high prestige and tends to be treated as the standard for Arakan. It is not a blanket description of all Arakanese varieties.

Both Okell's Intha and Tavoyan phoneme inventories include medial /l/ with restricted onset combinations, and Okell explicitly notes that Tavoyan /-l/ is absent from Standard Burmese. The two regional inventories are not identical; this combined claim records only the shared presence of /l/ and its absence from SB.

The 2008 SEAlang project description states that Burmese dictionary queries may be entered in local orthography, IPA phonetic form, or both, and its Burmese dictionary screenshot displays IPA transliterations alongside Burmese headwords and definitions. This confirms IPA input/display at the interface level, but not the internal storage format of the underlying dictionary records.
scope: pp.1-2; PDF lines 26-35

claim: The 2008 SEAlang project description shows that the Burmese dictionary interface accepts IPA phonetic queries and displays IPA transliterations, but it does not specify whether IPA is stored in the underlying dictionary records or generated from another representation. claim: Nishi states that his phonemic notation follows Okell (1995) and differs from Okell (1969), but explicitly says in footnote 3 that all examples in the paper are quoted from Okell (1969), Reference Grammar §§17–20; example provenance and transcription convention must therefore be kept distinct.
scope: Nishi 1998 p.253 lines 37–46 and note 3 pp.256–257 lines 323–330

claim: Nishi treats atonicization as unpredictable and sometimes optional and argues that it should not be stated together with the voicing sandhi rule; the project must keep the atonicization condition and consonant voicing process as separate operations.
scope: Nishi 1998 p.254 lines 120–124; historical discussion pp.254–255

claim: Nishi reports no phonemic voicing sandhi in Intha, Taungyo and Danu; only the first pattern in Arakanese, Tavoy and Mergui; and both first and second patterns in Yaw, though not in all contexts where Standard Burmese has voicing. The Taungyo evidence discussed is Minor Taungyo.

Nishi leaves several Standard Burmese voicing exceptions unexplained and tentatively discusses analogy, borrowing and Written Burmese influence; he characterizes the first sandhi pattern as drift or convergence rather than a feature traceable to one common origin.

Nishi (1997) explicitly limits the paper's detailed treatment to Burmese rhyme writing systems, referring to initials only when necessary; its historical medial observations are partial orthographic evidence, not a comprehensive medial inventory or a modern grapheme-to-phoneme specification.
scope: Nishi 1997 p.976, §0 Introduction, PDF lines 32–36

claim: Duan and Zhu (2025) propose a compound Burmese tone analysis with four traditional tone classes split into eight yin/yang categories (1a-4a and 1b-4b), distributed across modal and lower/breathy registers and analyzed through pitch, register/phonation and length. This is an author-proposed analysis, not a project-wide consensus.

Duan and Zhu (2025) report five speakers aged 22-38: two from Yangon, two from Taunggyi and one from the Mandalay region. Their word list contains 89 items (80 monosyllabic and 9 disyllabic with the target tone on the second syllable), read twice, yielding 694 valid word tokens. The sample is mixed-region, not a Yangon-only sample.
scope: §1.2, p.392; Appendices A-B

claim: Duan and Zhu (2025) report individual and inter-speaker variation, especially in tone classes T1 and T3, and discuss variation in relation to possible ongoing sound change and dialectal or individual differences. A single invariant pitch contour should not be assumed from this source.
scope: §5.3, Figure 7; discussion of T1/T3 variation

claim: Okell (1999) distinguishes the regular Burmese open/closed syllable system from added finals used to represent final consonants in non-Burmese words and names; these added-final sequences must not be imported as ordinary native Burmese rimes.
scope: ISO/IEC WG2 N2033, Appendix 2 pp.14-18; especially pp.14-15

claim: Okell (1999) reports that added finals can follow regular finals and tone marks, sometimes with two or three finals in a syllable; he argues that listing possible syllable endings is insufficient for boundary detection and suggests identifying the beginnings of new syllables instead. This is a text-processing proposal, not by itself a phonological syllabification rule.
scope: ISO/IEC WG2 N2033, §4 p.4 and Appendix 2 pp.14-15

claim: Okell (1999) describes different orthographic tone-mark arrangements for open and closed Burmese syllables: open vowels carry tone values explicitly or implicitly, while in closed syllables the vowel sign is treated as tone-free and absence of an explicit tone mark indicates low tone in the described regular system. This is orthographic encoding evidence, not a resolution of the modern four-vs-eight phonological tone analysis.
scope: ISO/IEC WG2 N2033, §§3-5 pp.2-5; Appendix 2 pp.14-15

claim: Hill (2019) describes Old Burmese medials y-, r- and l-; he treats medial -w- as arising from vowel breaking of -o1- to -wa- during the Old Burmese period and excludes it from the historical medial inventory. Limited evidence for double medials kry-, khly-, ply- and mly- is noted but excluded from the main inventory figure.
scope: §46, pp.48-49, Figure 2.3; discussion cites Nishi 1999 pp.1-10

claim: Hill (2019) defines Written Burmese as an idealized dictionary spelling standard that approximates pronunciation of the fourteenth century but reflects no specific time or place; historical medial -l- is lost, merging with -y- after velars and -r- after labials. These are historical correspondences, not modern Unicode-to-IPA mappings.

Hill (2019) states that Old Burmese did not regularly mark tones; sporadic tonal spellings exist, and he projects Written Burmese tone marking backwards onto Old Burmese for purposes of historical reconstruction. This is an explicit analytical reconstruction choice, not direct evidence that Old Burmese texts consistently marked tone.

Hill (2019) cautions that Old Burmese philological evidence is sparse and early inscriptional orthography unstable; his Old Burmese onset inventory is expressly subject to revision. Historical inventory figures must retain this source-level uncertainty.

Cornell University Library finding aid for the Nicholas C. Bodman Papers (Collection 14-13-3031) lists a July 1977 copy of Yoshio Nishi, Medials in Burmese, in Box 8, Folder 148, pages 41-52. This verifies a physical archival copy and its pagination, but not online full-text access or the contents of the paper.
scope: Cornell University Library finding aid, Container List, Box 8 Folder 148; consulted 2026-11-13

claim: Catalogues identify Okell (1969) as a two-volume work: volume 1 comprises pages xvii and 1-240, and volume 2 pages 241-482. The guide South East Asia: A Guide to Reference Material identifies volume 1 as Sounds and volume 2 as an alphabetical list of particles and common words. The requested §§17-20 are cited by Nishi (1998), but their text remains inaccessible in this review.
scope: Indiana University catalogue; Open Library edition records; Glottolog; South East Asia: A Guide to Reference Material entry 654

The romanization is therefore non-injective at this inventory level; retain the original Myanmar source-unit identity and never reverse-map an MLCTS string to a unique Burmese spelling. The collisions do not by themselves prove that the source spellings are interchangeable or homophonous.

The project's 94-row inventory takes the MLCTS column (array index 1), not MLCTS2 (array index 2). These two representations must not be conflated.

Preserve its context-sensitive status pending a primary orthographic/phonological analysis.

This is a nomenclature discrepancy within the software documentation, not evidence of two different data columns. Crosswalks should state the alias and must not call the column an MLC-primary transcription table.

claim: Allott reports that the MLC Concise Burmese Dictionary was published in five parts, with the first appearing in late 1978 and the last in 1980; she says it established official orthography for its entries and gave pronunciations. This identifies an earlier primary lexicographic source worth inspecting, but the article does not reproduce its pronunciation key or establish MLCTS/MLCTS2.

claim: Okell’s 1982 bibliography lists the MLC Concise Burmese Dictionary as five volumes, 1978-1980, Rangoon, Mranmācā Aphwai. This is an independent bibliographic locator for the earlier MLC monolingual dictionary, not direct access to its contents.

claim: A reproducible exact Unicode word-final string match over the MOW v0.1.3 Burmese lemma release (1,476 mya:lemma rows; 1,041 distinct lemma forms) finds 508 source-unit/lemma pairs across 35 of the 50 collision source-unit variants, representing 442 distinct lemma strings and 547 synsets. Both sides of 11/25 collision groups occur in this small wordnet, one side only in 13/25, and neither side in 1/25. This is orthographic lexical coverage only: MOW supplies no pronunciation here, suffix matching does not perform Burmese syllabification, and absence is not evidence of nonexistence. Do not treat these counts as confirmation of homophony, MLCTS correctness, or Ukrainian output.
scope: Official MOW v0.1.3 TSV, rows tagged mya:lemma; exact Unicode string endsWith against the 50 source_unit strings in romanization_rime_collisions.csv; generated 2026-11-13; upstream Git blob SHA 0c97fc4e98b3827dae0bc667858993037496ca58

claim: R12A’s secondary Burmese rhyme table supports a structured comparison for 21 of the 25 Mya2Rom MLCTS collision groups: 18 pairs receive the same IPA value in the table, three pairs (any, any:, any.) receive distinct values, two groups (ui, un) have only one side represented, a. is not listed, and u. is a special non-rime context fallback. For any, the table gives ဉ် as ɪ̀N but ည် as ì/è/ɛ̀; its explanatory text explicitly notes that အည် is not nasalised while ဉ has come to be used to produce nasalisation. The source table is a secondary descriptive synthesis, uses N as an archiphoneme, does not account for vowel reduction, and cites Wikipedia for part of its phonology inventory. It is not a primary MLC table or independent adjudicated lexical evidence; no runtime or Ukrainian mapping should be promoted from it.
scope: Richard Ishida, Myanmar (Burmese) Orthography Notes, updated 2026-04-28; §Additional phonetic details > Rhymes, lines 525-570; coda N explanation lines 207-214; closed nasal syllables and ည်/ဉ explanation lines 610-625; source note line 142

claim: The 2004 Myanmar Unicode and NLP Research Center national contribution to ISO/IEC JTC1/SC2/WG2 states that the Myanmar Language Commission published Myanmar Orthography in October 1986 and that the Ministry of Education prescribed it by notification as the national standard. It describes four basic medial signs and combinations yielding eleven medial symbols, and explains that medials alter pronunciation and are structurally distinct from stacked consonants. This is evidence for orthographic/structural analysis only; the proposal is not the MLC book itself and supplies no MLCTS or IPA rime table.
scope: WG2 N2827, §§D.1-D.5.1, lines 273-320; title/administrative status lines 0-15, 21-35
